The Earth goes around the sun in a big path called an orbit, and it takes one year to complete this journey. But here’s the cool part: the Earth isn’t straight up and down as it orbits. It’s tilted at an angle, like a spinning top! This tilt is what causes the seasons.  

When the Northern Hemisphere (where we live) is tilted toward the sun, it gets more sunlight and warmer weather. That’s summer! But when it’s tilted away from the sun, it gets less sunlight and cooler weather—winter. The Southern Hemisphere experiences the opposite seasons at the same time.  

In between, we have spring and fall. Spring happens when the Earth starts tilting toward the sun, and fall is when it starts tilting away. The amount of daylight changes too—summer has longer days, and winter has shorter ones.

Einstein and others considered such behavior impossible, as it violated the local realism view of causality (Einstein referring to it as "spooky action at a distance") and argued that the accepted formulation of quantum mechanics must therefore be incomplete.
